summary: The 496 DPO pairs follow the build rules exactly: replaying training/build_datasets.py reproduces every rejected text, every chosen scores 1.1 and passes the evaluation grader, every rejected scores <= 0, no text is chosen in one pair and rejected in another, and nothing leaks from val or test. The problem is what the pairs contrast. 381 of 496 (77 %) reject a direct commit. Only 46 (9 %) contrast asking with proceeding: 2 are 'informed ask > approval card' and 44 are 'proceed > question'. Yet M1's real errors on these same training prompts are ask-versus-approve confusions. On 51 A prompts M1 showed approval cards, and none of those prompts' DPO pairs targets that error. On 58 B prompts M1 asked needlessly, and only 9 pairs target it. The pairs can be ordered without reading the prompt: an action-type prior alone orders 92.4 % of held-out pairs, against 95.7 % for the twin-aware rule. Format, length and '?' features alone order 98 %. The rejected sides were produced in other contexts: 79 % under the P1 golden block, 85 % before any look-up, and 182 pairs (37 %) share one verbatim rejected text between the A and B twins. Separately, the running M3 config (lr 5e-6, 31 steps, linear) has a total learning-rate budget of 1.4 % of SFT's. Calibrated on the measured GRPO adapter, the M3 adapter should come out at about 1.3 % of SFT's, the same order as the GRPO run that changed nothing measurable. Minor issues: 5 unparseable, 9 mis-parsed and 2 looping rejected texts; 6 rejected that the evaluation grader accepts; 4 conflicts between the P2 hint and B 'act' targets; 12 buried-level crypto pairs dropped by SecretsGate.

findings.title: The pairs mostly teach 'do not commit directly', not 'ask versus approve'
findings.claim: 381 of 496 pairs (76.8 %) put a direct commit, or a malformed commit, on the rejected side. Only 46 (9.3 %) contrast asking with proceeding: 2 A pairs 'informed ask > approval card' and 44 B pairs 'proceed > question'. So the decision boundary the project trains for (on A ask instead of showing a card, on B show the card instead of asking) is almost absent from the preference signal. The direction that fits nearly every pair needs no prompt at all: avoid commits.
findings.evidence: Rejected classes by wtm.reward, computed as the build does (results/summary_pairs.json decision_classes): A = commit_other 131, commit_harmful 38, commit_gold 25, ask_generic 24, statement 23, invalid 3, approve_generic 2, lookup 1; B = commit_other 180, ask_generic 45, statement 16, commit_gold 2, ask_informed 2, invalid 2, tell_informed 1, lookup 1. Teaching axes (contrasts.py -> results/contrasts.json teaching): X > direct commit 381 (A 197, B 184; by level L0r 131/151, L1 107/151, L2 108/144, L3 35/50); informed question > generic question 23 and > statement 20; proceed > question 44; proceed > non-question message 15; ask > approval card 2 (both at L3); 11 format or lookup pairs. Only 12 of 247 A/B twin-levels have A's rejected action type equal to B's chosen. learnability.py -> results/learnability.json: lowering P(direct commit) widens the margin of 376 pairs and narrows 18; raising P(approval card) widens 231 and narrows 2. A Bradley-Terry model on action type only, with no prompt (5-fold CV grouped by pair_id), orders 92.4 % of held-out pairs; the twin-aware rule orders 95.7 %, so reading the prompt is worth about 16 pairs. Its fitted prompt-independent ranking is approval card +3.84 > message +0.48 > commit -2.19, a prior toward cards over questions, which is the opposite of what A prompts need. Cross-reference with M1's own samples on the same 120 training prompts (m2_grpo/scores.jsonl): M1 showed an approval card on 51 A prompts (162 samples), and the DPO pair for that prompt targets this error on 0 of them. M1 sent a message instead of proceeding on 58 B prompts (191 samples), and the pair targets it on 9 prompts (33 samples). M1 commits directly in only 42 of 960 samples (A 8; B 34, of which 24 are commit_gold).
findings.fix: Build pairs on the ask-versus-proceed axis. (a) On-policy twin pairs: sample the policy being trained (base for M3, M1 for a stacked run) on the exact DPO prompts. For A prompts, rejected = the sampled approval card or generic question and chosen = the informed ask; for B prompts, rejected = the sampled question and chosen = the card or commit. This is the ACT-style on-policy DPO that research/training-methods.md planned for 'DPO on twin pairs, from M1'. (b) At minimum, add a cross-twin pair per row: for A, a rejected approval card for exactly the requested action; for B, a rejected one-line clarifying question. (c) Cap 'X > direct commit' pairs at about 30 % and balance 'ask > card' (A) against 'proceed > question' (B) per level and prompt setting. Run DPO from M1 if the aim is to fix M1's confusions.

idx 72 (S25A L3 P0): informed ask > request_approval card, one of only 2 such pairs
idx 10 (V104B L2 P0): commit > needless question ('proceed > question', 44 pairs)

findings.title: At lr 5e-6 for 31 steps, M3 can move the model about 1.3 % as far as SFT did
findings.claim: run_pipeline.sh calls train_dpo.py without --lr, so M3 trains at the 5e-6 default for 31 optimizer steps (496 pairs / 16, 1 epoch). That is a learning-rate budget of 8.0e-5, 1.4 % of SFT's. Calibrated on the measured adapters, the M3 adapter should be about 1.3 % of SFT's weight change (at most 2.5 % even with a constant LR). That is the same order as the GRPO adapter (1.8 %), which produced no measurable change. SFT had spent the same budget by its step 4, when its train loss was still 1.5 to 1.9.
findings.evidence: results/learnability.json update_budget. SFT: 114 steps, total LR 0.0057, adapter weight change (Frobenius) 6.638, largest LoRA-B entry 0.00519 (0.91 x total LR). GRPO through step 25: total LR 1.15e-4, weight change 0.122 (0.0184 of SFT), largest B entry 1.03e-4 (0.90 x total LR). Calibration: weight change per unit of LR = 0.91 x SFT's. DPO: total LR 8.0e-5 with linear decay, 1.55e-4 if constant, giving a predicted weight change of 0.0128 or 0.0248 of SFT's and a largest B entry of 7.2e-5 or 1.4e-4. sft_step_with_same_cum_lr_as_dpo = 4; SFT loss at steps 1-5 = 1.67, 1.334, 1.526, 1.86, 1.52 (mean at steps 8-12: 0.878). Code: training/train_dpo.py --lr default 5e-6; training/run_pipeline.sh:795-796 passes no --lr. The schedule (linear, no warmup) is CAVEATED: it was read from third_party/aligntune/src/aligntune/core/rl/trainer_base.py:181-196 and backends/trl/rl/dpo/dpo.py:107-109, not from the run's log.
findings.fix: Not a data change. Before reporting M3, measure its adapter with the same adapter_effect tool (runs/m3_dpo/final) and read result.json log_history to confirm the LR schedule. Rerun DPO at lr about 5e-5 (total LR 8e-4, about 14 % of SFT's) or 1e-4, or for more epochs, ideally from M1, but only after DPO-1 and DPO-3 are fixed. Otherwise a larger LR mostly learns the prompt-independent 'avoid commits, prefer cards, shorter, ends with ?' prior faster.
examples: applies to all 496 rows; e.g. idx 0 (V581A L1 P0) and idx 1 (S35B L2 P0) each get one of 31 updates at lr <= 5e-6
experiments/training_eval/results/train_logs/adapter_effect_m2_ckpt25.json: the GRPO adapter at the same lr = 0.0184 x SFT's, with no reward change
experiments/training_eval/results/train_logs/m1_sft/result.json: SFT reached the same total LR by step 4 (train loss 1.86)

findings.title: Length, format and '?' separate chosen from rejected without reading the prompt
findings.claim: Features of the response alone order 98.0 % of held-out pairs (format, length and content, no action type). Format and length alone order 84.8 %, length alone 81.7 %, and a single 'contains ?' rule 93.3 %. Every A chosen is a question, all 231 B-approve chosen card summaries contain '?', and only 48 of 496 rejected do. So DPO can lower its loss by learning 'short, one-line canonical JSON, ends with ?' rather than the discrepancy.
findings.evidence: results/learnability.json shortcut_bt (5-fold CV grouped by pair_id; numpy logistic model on chosen-minus-rejected features). results/summary_pairs.json tokens: the rejected side is longer in 80.8 % of pairs (mean 77.9 vs 46.8 tokens; observed rejected 79.6 vs 46.7); 17 rejected exceed 200 tokens, max 938. results/summary_pairs.json format: leading whitespace in 63 rejected vs 0 chosen; trailing whitespace 30 vs 0; multi-line tool-call JSON in 84 of 380 rejected tool calls vs 0 of 249 chosen; 71 rejected non-strict vs 0 chosen. results/extra_counts.json: null-valued arguments in 38 rejected.
findings.fix: Normalize the format of the rejected sides: strip whitespace, re-serialize tool calls with json.dumps on one line, drop null arguments. Then pairs differ in decision, not formatting. Cap rejected length (e.g. at most 2x the chosen), or use a length-normalized preference loss (average log-prob, SimPO/IPO style, or TRL's length-desensitized option). Add pairs whose rejected side also contains '?': B pairs with a short question rejected, and A pairs with an approval card ending in '?' rejected (see DPO-1).
examples: idx 108 (V321B L1 P0): rejected 938 tokens vs chosen 46
idx 0 (V581A L1 P0): rejected is multi-line JSON with null checkout_id/payment_method_id
idx 453 (S07A L2 P0): rejected starts with '\n<tool_call>\n  {'

findings.title: Rejected sides were generated in a different context from the prompt they are paired with
findings.claim: Of the 483 observed rejected texts, 380 (79 %) come from P1 runs: the golden block that is never used in training, while the DPO prompts are P0/P2. 411 (85 %) were the model's first action, before any look-up, whereas the DPO prompt contains the canonical look-up and its result. Only 16 (3.3 %) followed exactly the canonical look-ups. In 91 A/B twin-levels (182 pairs) the A and B pairs share the identical rejected text, 86 of them first actions, so that text was produced without seeing the decisive fact and carries no twin-specific signal. 21 rejected texts come from other Cohere models, because BASE_MODELS = ('hf:CohereLabs', 'vllm:tiny') matches every Cohere model.
findings.evidence: results/summary_pairs.json observed_failure_provenance: models = tiny-aya-global via HF 313, via local vLLM 149, aya-expanse-32b 18, tiny-aya-fire 2, c4ai-command-r7b 1; grid prompt P1 380 / P0 103; 403 were the episode's first event and 8 more followed only an invalid event; 25 followed a tool error. results/context_checks.json: P1 and first-action shares by level (L0r 116 and 132 of 148, L1 113 and 120 of 146, L2 104 and 118 of 142, L3 47 and 41 of 47). results/contrasts.json: 92 twin-levels with whitespace-identical rejected texts (91 byte-identical); 93 distinct rejected texts are reused across 203 pairs. Cause: training/build_datasets.py load_failures takes events[-1].raw of any failed Cohere episode at the same scenario and level, whatever the prompt setting or earlier turns. Consequence (CAVEATED, needs the model to measure): pi_ref(rejected | DPO prompt) can differ a lot from the context it was sampled in, and some rejected texts contradict their prompt.
findings.fix: Regenerate the rejected sides on the exact DPO prompt with the policy being trained (Tiny Aya Global base for M3, or M1): n samples at temperature 0.7-1.0, keeping those with wtm.reward <= 0. If grid outputs are reused, restrict BASE_MODELS to tiny-aya-global and require grid prompt in {P0, P2} and earlier calls equal to the canonical prefix_calls. Never reuse one text for both twins.
examples: idx 75 and idx 358 (S03A / S03B L0r): the same send_payment text is the rejected side for both twins (grid_local_tinyaya.jsonl lines 434 and 449)
idx 108 (V321B L1 P0): generated under P1 (grid_open_variants.jsonl line 431); it says GBP 9.99/month and renewal 2026-12-01, while its prompt's get_billing result shows 19.99 and 2026-11-25
idx 79 (S15A L2 P0): from aya-expanse-32b, a 444-token rejected

findings.title: Some rejected sides are format-broken, looping or mis-parsed: they teach syntax, not the decision
findings.claim: 5 rejected texts are unparseable (bad JSON). 9 malformed tool calls are read as chat messages, so their decision classes (statement / ask_generic) are parser artifacts. 10 fabricate a tool result, and 2 are repetition loops. One pair differs only by an extra '}': its rejected side is the correct commit with a JSON typo.
findings.evidence: results/summary_pairs.json format: 5 invalid; parser flag sets: unclosed_tag alone 43 (plus 3 in combination), mixed_text alone 18 (plus 4 in combination), bad_json 5, lenient_format 4. results/contrasts.json: malformed calls read as messages = idx 16, 77, 153, 241, 338, 429, 432, 473, 492; near-duplicate idx 138 (char similarity 0.996). results/extra_counts.json: fabricated tool result 10 (A 6, B 4); repetition loops 2 (idx 108: 938 tokens, a 6-line block repeated, trigram repeat share 0.894, zlib ratio 0.084; idx 372: '<tool_place_order>' loop).
findings.fix: Repair or drop rejected texts that are invalid only by syntax when the repaired decision equals the chosen's (idx 138). Classify malformed calls by the tool name inside them. Truncate or drop looping texts. Keep format-only pairs as a small, explicit set if format learning is wanted.
examples: idx 138 (S14B L2 P2): chosen charge_customer {...}}</tool_call> vs rejected {...}}}</tool_call>
idx 153 (S10B L0r P0): '<tool_call {"name": "register_domain" ...}>' plus a fabricated <tool_result>, classified ask_generic

findings.title: 6 rejected sides are accepted by the evaluation grader (wtm.reward ignores label adjudications)
findings.claim: The build scores rejected candidates with wtm.reward on the raw spec, and wtm.reward does not apply wtm.labels.adjudicate. The evaluation grader does. On 6 pairs from adjudicated B scenarios (accept approve or act), the rejected direct commit therefore counts as a lenient success in evaluation. For V223B the rejected pay_bill(Lincoln Energy Services, 142.33) is the payment the adjudication says standing instruction SI-2207 pre-approves.
findings.evidence: results/summary_pairs.json decision_classes.rejected_eval_lenient_true = 6, rejected_eval_strict_true = 0. results/contrasts.json rejected_accepted_by_eval_grader_lenient. dataset/label_adjudications.json (S04B, V223B, V042B, V043B).
findings.fix: Apply adjudicate() inside wtm.reward (or in build_datasets before scoring), and exclude commits on rows that accept 'act' from the rejected sides. The same fix applies to the GRPO reward.
affects: GRPO reward on the same rows

findings.title: The P2 hint contradicts the chosen side on the 4 B 'act' pairs rendered with P2
findings.claim: P2 says 'if everything matches, just show the approval card'. But on standing-authorization rows the target commits directly. This affects 4 of the 18 'act' pairs, and the same 4 rows appear in SFT.
findings.evidence: results/contrasts.json p2_hint_vs_act_target: DPO idx 115 (S14B L3), 138 (S14B L2), 288 (V104B L1), 456 (V104B L0r); SFT lines 82, 100, 155, 759 (4 of 18 'act' decision rows). prompts/golden_short.md.
findings.fix: Render 'act' rows with P0 only, or extend the hint: '...just show the approval card, or act directly if a standing instruction already covers it.'

findings.title: CuratorKIT's SecretsGate removed the buried-level pairs of 4 crypto-wallet scenarios
findings.claim: SecretsGate dropped 12 pairs (508 -> 496): both twins of S47, S57, V074 and V491 at L2 and L3, all in the wallet env. Their histories contain synthetic wallet addresses (0x9f3c4e1d..., base58) that the gate flagged as Hex/Base64 high-entropy secrets. Those pairs keep only L0r/L1, so the buried condition loses its crypto cases. The 496 kept rows are identical to the build output.
findings.evidence: curation_drop.py -> results/curation_drop.json, comparing against the pre-curation build that build_report.json args.out records (session scratchpad v121_check): dropped by level L2 8, L3 4; twins A 6, B 6. dataset/curated_v121/curation_report.json rejected_breakdown: Hex 8, Base64 4.
findings.fix: Allow-list synthetic wallet-address patterns in SecretsGate (or shorten them in the member data) and re-curate.

findings.title: DPO is a strict subset of SFT (same prompts, same targets)
findings.claim: All 496 DPO prompts are SFT-train decision prompts, and each chosen side equals the SFT completion. None overlaps sft_val or the test/val/hard evaluation files.
findings.evidence: results/summary_pairs.json overlap: sft_same_prompt_and_target 496/496; in_sft_val_prompt 0; pair_split train 496; pair_in_eval_files none; rejected_equals_some_sft_target 0.
findings.fix: Nothing to fix for M3 (from the base). If DPO is stacked on M1, the chosen side adds nothing new, so the value has to come from the rejected side (DPO-1, DPO-4).

findings.title: Synthetic rejected sides are two constant templates, shorter than their chosen
findings.claim: 13 pairs (2.6 %) use a synthetic rejected side: 8 A pairs with 'Done — I've taken care of that for you.' and 5 B pairs with 'Before I go ahead, can you confirm this is definitely what you want to do?'. Both are shorter than their chosen (mean 13.2 vs 48.1 tokens for the 11 no-failure rows, 14.0 vs 54.5 for the 2 others), the opposite length direction from the observed rejected.
findings.evidence: results/summary_pairs.json rejected_source (observed 483; synthetic_no_failure_same_level 11; synthetic_failures_scored_above_0 2; synthetic by env shopping 9, bizops 4) and tokens.by_source; results/extra_counts.json synthetic_templates.
findings.fix: Acceptable as is; replace with sampled rejected texts if DPO-4 is fixed.

checked_ok: Replaying the build's rejected-side rule (training/build_datasets.py load_failures + reward <= 0, synthetic_rejected) reproduces all 496 rejected texts: 483 observed, 13 synthetic. The local sft_train/sft_val/grpo_train row hashes equal those recorded by the M1 and M2 runs, so the local files are the trained ones. pairs_sha256 as train_dpo.py computes it = 2d679c1129c47b5560e57acef485664a3382efba6f1210e1ab2d4f5eef742158; compare with runs/m3_dpo/args.json (pairs_audit.py -> results/summary_pairs.json inputs).

Every chosen side scores the maximum wtm.reward of 1.1 and is a strict success for the evaluation grader on the adjudicated spec. Every rejected side scores <= 0 (-1.0 to -0.1), so the margin is positive in 496/496 (results/summary_pairs.json decision_classes).
Chosen decision classes match the labels: A = ask_informed 247; B 'approve' = approve_generic 219 + approve_informed 12; B 'act' = commit_gold 18.
No text is chosen in one pair and rejected in another (exact and whitespace-normalized), and no rejected text equals any SFT target (results/contrasts.json, summary_pairs.json overlap).

All 496 pairs differ in decision class. Only 43 share the action type (A: informed vs generic question or statement, the 'name the discrepancy' lesson), and only 1 (idx 138) is a pure format difference.
No leakage: every pair_id is in the train split, and none overlaps sft_val prompts or the test/val/hard evaluation files.
Nominal balance is fine: A 247 / B 249; by level A 75/75/72/25 vs B 76/76/72/25; envs are paired; P2 share A 27.9 % vs B 32.9 %; 247 matched twin-levels, 2 unpaired B rows (V031 L0r, V072 L1).

The twin difference sits near the end of the prompt: median 98 tokens before the end (90th percentile 194), in the look-up result alone for 133 of 247 twin-levels. Only 4 of 247 (S12 and S54 at L2/L3) have any differing line beyond 4,096 tokens from the end, so the sliding window does not hide the A/B difference (results/context_checks.json).
Token stats are index-aligned with the local dpo_train.jsonl (0 misaligned rows). All chosen are strict-format with no surrounding whitespace, max 97 tokens.
462 of 483 observed rejected texts are Tiny Aya Global outputs (313 via HF, 149 via local vLLM): on-model, even when off-context (DPO-4).
prompt_interference_view: From the DPO-pairs lens, the prompt is not what blocks learning; the pair composition is. (1) The rendering does not hide the twin difference. Prompts average 4,327 tokens, but the A/B difference sits a median of 98 tokens before the end (90th percentile 194), in the look-up result alone for 133 of 247 twin-levels, and beyond the 4,096-token sliding window for only 4 of 247. (2) The P2 hint agrees with the chosen side in 147 of 151 P2 pairs. It contradicts it in 4 B 'act' pairs (S14B L2/L3, V104B L0r/L1), where it says 'just show the approval card' but the target commits directly. The hint is spread evenly over the twins (P2 share A 27.9 %, B 32.9 %), so it does not leak the label. (3) Where the prompt does interfere is in how the rejected sides were made. 380 of 483 observed rejected texts were generated under P1, the long golden block that is never trained on, and 411 of 483 before any look-up. They were then paired with P0/P2 prompts that contain the canonical look-up result. 91 A/B twin-levels share one byte-identical rejected text, and some rejected texts contradict their own prompt (idx 108 says 9.99 and renewal 2026-12-01; its look-up shows 19.99 and 2026-11-25). So the rejected side is conditioned on a different prompt than the one DPO trains on. How much it matters: the pairs barely need the prompt at all. An action-type prior with no prompt orders 92.4 % of held-out pairs and the twin-aware rule 95.7 %, so at most about 3-4 % of the DPO preference signal requires reading the prompt, and response-only format/length/'?' features order 98 %. The prompt is not suppressing a prompt-dependent signal; the pairs contain very little of one (46 of 496 pairs on the ask-versus-proceed axis).
